books.argument: Agamemnon and Achilles quarrel over Briseis; Achilles withdraws, and Zeus is petitioned.

scenes.summary: The poet invokes the Muse to sing the wrath of Achilles and its cost.
Chryses comes to ransom his daughter Chryseis; Agamemnon spurns and threatens the priest.
Chryses withdraws along the shore and prays to Apollo for vengeance.
Apollo descends in wrath, shoots mules and dogs first, then men; pyres of the dead burn continually.
For nine days the plague rages; on the tenth, Achilles calls an assembly, and Calchas names Chryseis its cause.
Agamemnon agrees to return Chryseis but demands another prize in compensation.
Achilles and Agamemnon trade bitter words; Agamemnon threatens to seize Briseis.
Achilles nearly draws his sword on Agamemnon; Athena, seen only by him, restrains his hand.
Achilles denounces Agamemnon and swears by his sceptre to withhold aid from the army.
Nestor urges reconciliation, recalling the Lapiths, and appeals to both men to yield.
The quarrel ends unresolved; the assembly disperses; Odysseus is sent to restore Chryseis.
Heralds Talthybius and Eurybates lead Briseis away from Achilles' tent.
Achilles weeps alone by the sea and calls on his mother Thetis for help.
Thetis rises from the sea to comfort Achilles and agrees to beg Zeus to honor him.
Odysseus reaches Chryse and restores Chryseis to her father Chryses.
The Achaeans sacrifice a hecatomb to Apollo, feast, sing a hymn, then sail home at dawn.
Achilles remains apart from the fighting, nursing his anger by the ships.
After twelve days Thetis ascends Olympus and wins Zeus's reluctant nod to honor Achilles.
Zeus returns to his throne; Hera, suspecting collusion with Thetis, confronts him sharply.
Hephaestus calms the gods with an old tale; they feast, laugh, and retire to sleep.

books.argument: Agamemnon tests the troops; Odysseus quells the panic; the opposing armies are catalogued.

scenes.summary: Zeus sends a deceptive Dream, in Nestor's likeness, urging Agamemnon to attack at once.
Agamemnon wakes and dresses in the dark as dawn rises over the camp.
Agamemnon convenes the council of elders, recounts the dream, and summons the full army.
The assembly gathers; Agamemnon tests resolve by proposing retreat, and the men rush for the ships.
Athena, sent by Hera, halts the rout; Odysseus restrains leaders with words, common men with blows.
Thersites alone rails on against the kings, mocking Agamemnon and Achilles.
Odysseus rebukes Thersites and strikes him with the sceptre; the army laughs approvingly.
Odysseus urges perseverance, recalling the omen of the snake and nine sparrows at Aulis.
The army shouts assent; Nestor urges Agamemnon to organize the host by tribe and phratry.
Agamemnon praises Nestor, laments Achilles' absence, and orders the meal before battle.
The army feasts after sacrifice; Agamemnon's prayer to Zeus goes unfulfilled as the host musters.
The poet invokes the Muses before naming the Achaean leaders and their ships.
Catalogue of Ships: Boeotian, central Greek, Athenian, and Salaminian contingents, with Diomedes' Argives.
Catalogue of Ships: Mycenae, Lacedaemon, Pylos, Arcadia, Elis, and the western-island contingents.
Catalogue of Ships: Aetolians, Cretans under Idomeneus, Rhodians under Tlepolemus, and nearby islands.
Catalogue of Ships: Achilles' idle Myrmidons, the leaderless men of slain Protesilaus, and Thessaly.
Ajax is named best of the Achaeans present, Eumelus' mares finest; the host advances like wildfire.
Iris warns Priam that the Achaeans approach; the Trojans hold an assembly.
The Trojans and their allies march out and array themselves on the plain.
Catalogue of the Trojans and their allies, arrayed under Hector and other leaders.

books.argument: Paris duels Menelaus for Helen; Aphrodite rescues him from defeat.

scenes.summary: The Trojans advance with cries like cranes; the Achaeans march on in disciplined silence.
Paris strides out as champion but shrinks back in fear at the sight of Menelaus.
Hector rebukes Paris for cowardice; Paris proposes a duel with Menelaus for Helen.
Hector announces the truce; Agamemnon accepts, and heralds are sent to fetch lambs and Priam.
Iris tells Helen of the coming duel; Helen goes to the wall, thinking of her past.
The teichoscopia begins: Priam asks Helen to name the tall warrior, and she answers.
Priam asks about Odysseus; Helen and Antenor describe his eloquence and bearing.
Priam asks about Ajax; Helen looks in vain for her brothers, already dead at home.
Heralds bring the oath-sacrifice lambs and wine, and Idaeus summons Priam to the field.
Priam rides out; Agamemnon swears the oath before Zeus, Sun, and Earth as witnesses.
Priam, unable to watch his son fight, returns to Troy.
Hector and Odysseus measure the ground and cast lots for who casts first.
Paris and Menelaus arm and advance, shaking their spears at one another in fury.
In the duel Menelaus shatters his sword and drags Paris by the helmet; Aphrodite snatches him away.
Aphrodite, disguised as an old woman, compels the reluctant Helen to go to Paris.
Helen reaches Paris's chamber and reproaches his cowardice; he urges her to bed instead.
As the two lie together, Menelaus searches the field for Paris; Agamemnon claims victory.

books.argument: The gods renew the war; Pandarus wounds Menelaus, breaking the truce; battle resumes.

scenes.summary: Zeus opens the divine council, provocatively suggesting the war end since Menelaus has won.
Hera demands Troy's destruction; Zeus yields but sends Athena down to break the truce.
Athena, disguised as Laodocus, persuades the Trojan archer Pandarus to shoot at Menelaus.
Pandarus looses his arrow; Athena deflects it, and Menelaus is wounded, his blood flowing.
Agamemnon, terrified for his brother, comforts him but voices dread of Troy's future taunts.
Menelaus reassures Agamemnon; Machaon is summoned and treats the wound with Chiron's herbs.
As Menelaus is tended, the Trojans advance and Agamemnon begins his review of the troops.
Agamemnon praises Idomeneus and the Cretans for their eagerness to fight.
Agamemnon praises the two Ajaxes, seeing their ranks arrayed and ready.
Agamemnon praises Nestor's skillful deployment of the Pylian chariots and foot.
Agamemnon rebukes Odysseus and Menestheus for seeming slack; Odysseus retorts angrily.
Agamemnon rebukes Diomedes, comparing him to his father; Sthenelus objects, but Diomedes stays silent.
The armies clash; a great simile likens the Achaean advance to surf breaking on shore.
Antilochus and Ajax open the killing; Simoisius falls, likened to a felled poplar tree.
Further Achaean and Trojan warriors fall as the close fighting intensifies.

books.argument: Diomedes' aristeia: he routs Trojans, wounds Aphrodite and Ares, aided throughout by Athena.

scenes.summary: Athena kindles fire-like courage in Diomedes and leads Ares from the battle.
Diomedes storms through the Trojan ranks like a flooding river, felling many warriors.
Pandarus wounds Diomedes; Athena restores his strength and sight to know gods from men.
Pandarus and Aeneas, dismayed by Diomedes, resolve to face him together in Aeneas's chariot.
Diomedes kills Pandarus with a spear through the face and wounds Aeneas with a great stone.
Aphrodite shields and rescues her son Aeneas; Diomedes wounds her hand and she flees.
Aphrodite, borrowing Ares' chariot, flees to Olympus and is comforted by her mother Dione.
Apollo shields Aeneas from Diomedes and restores him to the field, then rouses Ares to aid Troy.
Sarpedon rebukes Hector for holding back; Hector rejoins the fight as Ares spurs on the Trojans.
Aeneas, healed, rejoins the ranks; fierce fighting resumes with losses on both sides.
Hector, aided by Ares, cuts down several Achaeans as the Trojans press their advantage.
Sarpedon and Tlepolemus trade taunts and fight; each gravely wounds the other.
The dying Tlepolemus is borne from the field; the badly wounded Sarpedon fights on.
The Achaeans give ground on learning that Ares himself fights for the Trojans.
Alarmed, Hera persuades Zeus and arms her chariot with Athena to intervene for the Achaeans.
Hera and Athena descend to the field and rally the disheartened Achaeans and Diomedes.
Athena mounts Diomedes' chariot in Sthenelus's place and urges him to attack Ares directly.
Diomedes, guided by Athena's hand, wounds Ares with his spear; the god cries out in pain.
Ares flees to Olympus and complains to Zeus, who rebukes him but has Paeon heal his wound.

books.argument: Hector returns to Troy for prayers; meets Glaucus, then Andromache, before rejoining battle.

scenes.summary: Fighting continues; Menelaus spares the suppliant Adrestus, but Agamemnon orders him slain.
Helenus urges Hector to have the Trojan women supplicate Athena; Hector departs for the city.
Diomedes challenges the advancing Glaucus, wary he might be a god in disguise.
Glaucus answers with the leaves simile and recounts his lineage back to Bellerophon.
Diomedes recognizes an ancestral guest-friendship; the two agree not to fight and swap armor.
Hector reaches Troy; the women crowd around him, and he declines Hecuba's offer of wine.
Hector asks Hecuba to lead the women in offering Athena a robe; the goddess refuses the prayer.
Hector finds Paris idling with his armor and rebukes him for shirking the battle.
Helen laments and invites Hector to sit, but he declines, anxious to see his own household.
Paris promises to follow; Hector goes home but finds Andromache gone to the wall.
Hector hastens to the Scaean gates and meets Andromache and the nurse with their infant son.
Andromache recalls the deaths of her father and brothers and begs Hector to fight from the wall.
Hector answers that honor forbids retreat, dreading Andromache's future slavery above his own death.
Hector's son, frightened by the helmet, is calmed; Hector prays for him, then sends Andromache home—war is for men.
Andromache goes home weeping, looking back; her handmaids raise a lament for Hector as though he were already dead.
Paris arms and hastens through the city to rejoin Hector; the brothers reconcile and set out together for battle.

books.argument: Hector duels Ajax; armies truce to bury their dead and build the Achaean wall.

scenes.summary: Hector and Paris sally from Troy; Glaucus wounds Iphinous as Trojans kill two Achaeans.
Apollo and Athena meet at the oak tree and agree to end the day's fighting with a duel.
Helenus urges Hector to challenge an Achaean champion to single combat; Hector halts the Trojans.
Hector challenges any Achaean to single combat, vowing honorable treatment of the fallen either way.
Menelaus volunteers in shame at the Achaeans' silence; Agamemnon restrains him as unequal to Hector.
Nestor rebukes the Achaeans' fear, recalling his youthful duel with Ereuthalion.
Nine champions volunteer; lots are cast in Agamemnon's helmet to choose Hector's opponent.
The lot falls to Ajax; the Achaeans pray for his victory or an even match.
Ajax arms and advances; he and Hector exchange defiant boasts before the combat.
Ajax and Hector trade spear-casts, then wrestle and hurl boulders at each other's shields.
Heralds part the duelists at nightfall; Hector and Ajax exchange gifts and part as friends.
At a feast, Nestor proposes a truce to burn the dead and build a wall and trench.
In Troy, Antenor urges returning Helen; Paris refuses but offers treasure; Priam sends Idaeus at dawn.
At dawn, Idaeus relays Paris's offer; Diomedes rejects it; Agamemnon accepts only the burial truce.
Both sides gather and cremate their dead on the battlefield.
The Achaeans build a wall and dig a trench to defend their ships.
Poseidon protests the new wall to Zeus, who assures him it will be destroyed once the Achaeans sail home.
At night, the Achaeans feast on Lemnian wine while Zeus thunders ominously overhead.

books.argument: Zeus bars the gods from war; Trojans rout the Achaeans and camp on the plain.

scenes.summary: At dawn, Zeus assembles the gods and forbids any of them to aid either side in battle.
Athena voices pity for the Danaans; Zeus reassures her he does not mean it fully.
Zeus drives to Mount Ida to watch the battle from above.
Both armies arm and clash on the plain between the camp and the city.
At midday Zeus weighs the fates in golden scales and dooms the Achaeans; he thunders and hurls fire.
Paris wounds Nestor's horse; Diomedes rescues the old man and they attack Hector, killing his charioteer.
Zeus's thunderbolt drives Diomedes back; Nestor turns their chariot in retreat as Hector taunts him.
Hector rallies the Trojans, boasts of burning the ships, and urges on his horses by name.
Hera protests to Poseidon at the Trojan advance, but he declines to defy Zeus.
The Trojans press the Achaeans to the trench; Agamemnon prays and Zeus sends a favorable eagle omen.
Diomedes and Teucer strike down many Trojans; Hector wounds Teucer with a stone as Ajax shields him.
The Trojans push the Achaeans back to the ditch as Hector leads the pursuit.
Hera and Athena, pitying the Danaans, prepare to defy Zeus and intervene in the battle.
Hera and Athena arm for battle, but Zeus sends Iris to turn them back to Olympus.
Zeus rebukes Athena and Hera and foretells Hector's rampage will continue until Achilles returns and Patroclus falls.
The sun sets, ending the day's fighting.
Hector orders watch-fires lit to trap the Achaeans and plans to renew battle at dawn.
The Trojans camp on the plain, feasting by a thousand fires as they await dawn.

books.argument: Agamemnon's envoys offer Achilles rich gifts to return; he refuses to rejoin the fight.

scenes.summary: Panic grips the Achaeans at night; Agamemnon weeps and proposes abandoning the war.
Diomedes rebukes Agamemnon's despair and vows to keep fighting even alone.
Nestor counsels posting sentinels and holding a council of elders over supper.
Seven captains post sentinels between the trench and the wall.
At a feast of elders, Nestor urges Agamemnon to win back Achilles with gifts.
Agamemnon agrees, listing lavish gifts and offering his daughter in marriage to Achilles.
Nestor proposes an embassy of Phoenix, Ajax, and Odysseus; the Achaeans pray to Poseidon.
The envoys find Achilles playing the lyre; he welcomes them and orders a feast prepared.
Odysseus relays the Trojan threat and Agamemnon's gifts, urging Achilles to save the ships.
Achilles refuses the gifts, announces his plan to sail home, and reveals his choice between two fates.
Phoenix pleads with Achilles, recalling his own youth and exile after cursing his father.
Phoenix continues: Peleus raised him after his flight; he urges Achilles to respect the Prayers of Zeus.
Phoenix tells how Meleager's wrath nearly lost Calydon until his wife's pleading roused him.
Phoenix warns against a hardened heart; Achilles offers him a bed but refuses further persuasion.
Ajax speaks bluntly of Achilles's hard heart; Achilles agrees to fight only if Hector reaches his own ships.
The envoys depart; Phoenix beds down while Achilles and Patroclus retire with their women.
Odysseus reports Achilles's refusal to Agamemnon; Diomedes urges preparing for battle at dawn.

books.argument: Odysseus and Diomedes raid the Trojan camp by night, killing Dolon and Rhesus.

scenes.summary: Sleepless with worry, Agamemnon rises before dawn and arms himself.
Menelaus, also sleepless, arms and joins his brother to discuss the crisis.
Agamemnon sends Menelaus to rouse Ajax and Idomeneus while he seeks Nestor.
Agamemnon wakes Nestor; they resolve to check the sentinels and gather the council.
Nestor rouses Odysseus and Diomedes to join the night council.
The chiefs inspect the wakeful sentinels; Nestor proposes sending a spy into the Trojan camp.
Diomedes volunteers for the mission and chooses Odysseus as his companion.
The two arm themselves; a heron's cry is taken as a favorable omen from Athena.
Hector convenes his council; Dolon volunteers to spy for the promised horses of Achilles.
Odysseus and Diomedes spot Dolon, let him pass, then run him down.
Dolon is captured and, begging for ransom, reveals the Trojan dispositions and the camp of Rhesus.
Diomedes kills Dolon despite his information; the spoils are dedicated to Athena.
Diomedes slaughters the sleeping Thracians and King Rhesus while Odysseus frees the horses.
Athena warns Diomedes to retreat before another god rouses the Trojans.
Apollo rouses a Thracian kinsman of Rhesus, who discovers the slaughter and raises the alarm.
Odysseus and Diomedes escape with Rhesus's horses; Nestor and the Achaeans welcome them and hear their tale.

books.argument: Agamemnon's aristeia gives way to Trojan gains as Hector nears the ships.

scenes.summary: Zeus sends Strife to the ships, kindling the Achaeans' desire for battle over retreat.
Agamemnon arms in splendid bronze armor as Athena and Hera thunder in his honor.
The armies clash at dawn; Zeus favors the Trojans while the other gods hold back.
Agamemnon's aristeia begins: he kills Bienor, Oileus, and two sons of Priam.
Agamemnon kills Antimachus's two sons despite their pleas for ransom.
Agamemnon routs the Trojans, pursuing them toward the Scaean gates and the oak tree.
Zeus sends Iris to tell Hector to hold back until Agamemnon is wounded.
Hector rallies the Trojans as Agamemnon kills Iphidamas, son of Antenor.
Coön wounds Agamemnon avenging his brother; Agamemnon kills Coön too, then withdraws in pain.
Hector drives the Trojans forward as Agamemnon leaves; Odysseus rallies Diomedes to hold the line.
Diomedes's spear dents Hector's helmet; Hector rallies and flees by chariot, mocked by Diomedes.
Paris wounds Diomedes's foot with an arrow; Diomedes scorns him and withdraws to the ships.
Left alone, Odysseus kills several Trojans including Socus, who wounds him before dying.
Hearing Odysseus's cry, Menelaus and Ajax fight through and rescue him from the Trojans.
Ajax routs more Trojans; Paris wounds Machaon, whom Nestor drives to the ships.
Cebriones directs Hector toward Ajax's sector as Zeus makes Ajax falter and give ground.
Ajax retreats stubbornly under fire; Eurypylus aids him and is wounded by Paris in turn.
Achilles, watching from his ship, sends Patroclus to learn who Nestor carried from the field wounded.
At his hut, Nestor lists the wounded Achaean leaders and urges Patroclus to rouse Achilles or wear his armor.
Hurrying back, Patroclus stops to treat the wounded Eurypylus, delaying his return to Achilles.

books.argument: Hector breaches the Achaean wall and drives the Danaans back to their ships.

scenes.summary: The narrator foretells that Poseidon and Apollo will later sweep away the Achaean wall with rivers.
Fighting resumes at the wall; Hector presses on, but the trench blocks his horses.
Polydamas advises attacking on foot; Hector agrees and the Trojans dismount in five companies.
The five Trojan companies and their leaders, including Sarpedon and Glaucus, are named.
Asius alone keeps his chariot and drives for an open gate, where two Lapiths bar his way.
Asius storms the gate; the Lapiths hold firm as Achaeans hurl stones and Asius complains to Zeus.
The Lapiths refuse to yield; amid fire and grief among the gods, they cut down Damasus, Pylon, and other Trojans.
An eagle drops a writhing serpent among the Trojans, an ominous portent at the trench.
Polydamas interprets the omen as a warning and urges retreat from the ships.
Hector angrily dismisses the omen, insists on Zeus's promise, and threatens Polydamas with death.
The Trojans advance in a Zeus-sent dust storm; the two Ajaxes rally the Achaeans under a hail of stones.
Zeus rouses Sarpedon, who urges Glaucus to fight for the honor Lycia grants them.
Alarmed by Sarpedon's approach, Menestheus sends a herald to summon Ajax and Teucer.
Ajax kills Epicles and Teucer wounds Glaucus as Sarpedon tears open a breach in the battlement.
Ajax and Teucer strike at Sarpedon, driving him back without killing him.
The battle at the wall hangs even, like a weaver's honest scales, until Zeus favors Hector.
Hector hurls a boulder that shatters the gate; the Trojans pour through and rout the Achaeans among the ships.

books.argument: Poseidon secretly rallies the Achaeans while Idomeneus wins a bloody aristeia at the ships.

scenes.summary: Zeus turns his gaze from Troy toward the distant Thracians, Mysians, and Abii, trusting the gods stay clear.
Poseidon, pitying the Achaeans, descends from Samothrace, arms in gold, and drives his chariot to a hidden sea-cave.
scenes.location: the sea near Samothrace and Imbros

scenes.summary: Disguised as Calchas, Poseidon rouses the two Aiantes and other captains to hold the ships against Hector.
Poseidon rebukes the Achaeans' slackness; the Aiantes' companies lock shields into a dense unbroken line.
Hector's charge is checked at the packed Achaean line; Meriones' spear-cast at Deiphobus misses.
Teucer kills Imbrius, Hector kills Amphimachus; the Aiantes strip and behead Imbrius as Poseidon goes to rouse Idomeneus.
Idomeneus arms and meets Meriones fetching a spear; the two debate courage and head to the left flank.
Battle clashes anew as Zeus and Poseidon, opposed in purpose, each work grief for mortal warriors.
Idomeneus kills Othryoneus, then Asius; Antilochus kills Asius's charioteer and drives off his horses.
Deiphobus kills Hypsenor as Antilochus defends the body; Idomeneus, aided by Poseidon, kills the rooted Alcathous.
Idomeneus taunts Deiphobus, who fetches Aeneas; Aeneas kills Oenomaus instead, and Deiphobus's throw kills Ascalaphus.
Deiphobus and Meriones fight over Ascalaphus's helm; Meriones wounds Deiphobus's arm, and Polites leads him off.
Aeneas kills Aphareus, Antilochus kills Thoon; Adamas, wounded by Antilochus, is finished off by Meriones.
Helenus wounds Deipyrus; Menelaus and Helenus trade shots, wounding his hand; Menelaus then kills Peisander.
Menelaus strips Peisander and rails at Trojan insatiability; Meriones fatally wounds Harpalion, and Paris kills Euchenor in revenge.
Hector, unaware of losses on the left, presses the ships; Boeotians, Locrians, and Phthians hold the line.
scenes.location: the ships of Aias and Protesilaus

scenes.summary: Polydamas urges Hector to rally the bravest and take counsel, fearing Achilles; Hector agrees and departs.
Hector finds many leaders dead or wounded, rebukes Paris for absence, and both rejoin the fight.
The Trojans surge forward; Hector and Aias trade defiant speeches over an omen as the armies clash again.

books.argument: Hera seduces Zeus asleep on Ida while Poseidon secretly turns the battle for the Achaeans.

scenes.summary: Nestor, hearing the din of battle, arms himself and sees the Achaeans routed and the wall broken.
Nestor meets the wounded kings; Agamemnon despairs and proposes launching the ships to flee by night.
Odysseus sharply rebukes Agamemnon's plan as ruinous; Diomedes proposes the wounded leaders encourage the fighters from behind.
Poseidon, disguised as an old man, clasps Agamemnon's hand, shouts encouragement, and fills the Achaeans with strength.
Hera spies Zeus on Ida and resolves to seduce him; she adorns herself and asks Aphrodite's help.
Aphrodite lends Hera her charmed girdle of allurement, believing Hera's story about reconciling Oceanus and Tethys.
Hera flies to Lemnos and persuades Sleep, brother of Death, to lull Zeus, promising him a Grace as wife.
Hera and Sleep reach Ida; overcome with desire, Zeus lies with her and sleeps beneath a golden cloud.
Sleep hastens to tell Poseidon that Zeus sleeps; Poseidon, bearing a dread sword, leads the Achaeans against Hector.
Hector casts at Aias and misses; Aias fells him with a stone, and Trojans bear the stunned Hector away.
With Hector down, Aias son of Oileus kills Satnius; Polydamas and Aias trade kills over two more Trojans.
Acamas kills Promachus and taunts the Argives; Peneleos avenges him, killing Ilioneus and displaying his severed head.
The Achaeans, led by the greater Aias, strip Trojan spoils as Poseidon turns the tide of battle.

books.argument: Zeus revives Hector through Apollo and drives the Achaeans back to their ships.

scenes.summary: Zeus wakes on Ida, sees Hector fallen and the rout reversed, and angrily accuses Hera of scheming.
Hera swears she did not incite Poseidon; softened, Zeus sends her to summon Iris and Apollo.
Hera returns to Olympus and warns the feasting gods of Zeus's anger, provoking Ares' fury over Ascalaphus.
Athena disarms and restrains furious Ares, warning his revenge would provoke Zeus's wrath against all the gods.
Hera dispatches Iris and Apollo to Zeus on Ida; he orders Iris to make Poseidon quit the field.
Iris delivers Zeus's ultimatum to Poseidon; indignant at being ranked inferior, Poseidon yields and withdraws into the sea.
Zeus sends Apollo to revive Hector with the aegis and rout the Achaeans back toward the ships.
Apollo revives Hector, who charges again; the terrified Danaans, briefly rallied by Thoas, form a line against him.
Apollo, bearing the aegis before the Trojans, breaks the Achaean wall and casts down the trench, driving them back.
Patroclus, hearing the rout, leaves wounded Eurypylus to urge Achilles into the war as fighting nears the ships.
Hector nearly fires Aias's ship; Aias kills Caletor, but Hector kills Lycophron, and Zeus breaks Teucer's bowstring.
Teucer takes up spear and shield; Hector rallies the Trojans, declaring death in war no disgrace.
Named duels continue as Trojans and Achaeans trade kills; Hector chides Melanippus and leads him into the fight.
Menelaus urges Antilochus into battle; he kills Melanippus, but Hector's charge drives him back to the Achaean line.
Zeus drives the Trojans toward the ships; Nestor implores the Achaeans by their absent families to hold firm.
Athena clears the mist from Achaean eyes; Aias ranges the decks with a great pike, defying Hector's assault.
Hector seizes the stern of Protesilaus's ship and calls for fire; Aias, beset by darts, alone holds off the flames.

books.argument: Patroclus, wearing Achilles's armor, routs the Trojans, kills Sarpedon, and is slain by Hector.

scenes.summary: Patroclus, weeping, begs Achilles to let him lead the Myrmidons wearing his armor to save the ships.
Achilles agrees, recalling his grievance against Agamemnon, but orders Patroclus to drive off the Trojans and return.
Aias, exhausted and beset by darts, is disarmed by Hector's sword-stroke and forced back from the ships.
Trojans set fire to a ship; Achilles calls Patroclus to arm quickly while he gathers the Myrmidon host.
Achilles marshals the Myrmidons in five companies, rebukes their past grumbling, and spurs them on; Patroclus and Automedon arm.
Achilles opens Thetis's chest for his sacred cup, pours a libation, and prays to Zeus for Patroclus's safe return.
The Myrmidons, likened to wasps, charge; Patroclus kills the Paeonian leader Pyraechmes and quenches the fire on a ship.
Patroclus and the Danaan captains slay Trojan and Lycian warriors as the Trojans are pushed back over the trench.
Patroclus pursues Hector's fleeing chariot across the trench and slaughters Trojans trapped in the space near the wall.
Sarpedon rallies the Lycians against Patroclus; Zeus, pitying his doomed son, is dissuaded by Hera from saving him.
Patroclus kills Sarpedon's squire Thrasymelus, then Sarpedon himself, who dies urging Glaucus to defend his body.
Wounded Glaucus prays to Apollo for healing, then rallies the Lycians and Trojans to fight over Sarpedon's corpse.
Achaeans and Trojans battle fiercely over Sarpedon's body under gathering darkness that Zeus draws over the fight.
Meriones and Aeneas duel indecisively; Patroclus rebukes their boasting and presses the fight, driving the Trojans back.
Zeus, having let the Achaeans strip Sarpedon's armor, sends Apollo to bear the body home to Lycia.
Forgetting Achilles's warning, Patroclus kills many nearing the wall; Apollo thrice repels him, then, as Asius, spurs Hector on.
Patroclus kills Hector's charioteer Cebriones with a stone; Trojans and Achaeans battle over the corpse until evening favors the Achaeans.
Patroclus, killing thrice-nine Trojans, is stunned and stripped by Apollo, wounded first by Euphorbus's spear, then struck dead by Hector.
Hector, lion-like, vaunts over the dying Patroclus, who foretells his death by Achilles; his soul flees, and Hector pursues Automedon.

books.argument: Menelaus and Aias guard Patroclus's corpse through fierce fighting as Antilochus runs to warn Achilles.
where: the trench and the Achaean ships

scenes.summary: Menelaus stands guard over fallen Patroclus and kills Euphorbus, who had first speared him, in single combat.
Menelaus prepares to strip Euphorbus's armor, but Apollo incites Hector against him by pointing out the slain man.
Hector's fury drives Menelaus back from the corpse; he finds Aias and begs him to help save Patroclus's body.
Hector strips Patroclus's armor and withdraws as Aias arrives to guard the corpse; Glaucus begins rebuking Hector's cowardice.
Hector answers Glaucus, dons Achilles's stripped armor; Zeus marvels and grants him might; he promises spoils for Patroclus's body.
Aias fears for their lives; Menelaus summons the Danaan chiefs as fierce fighting resumes; Aias routs the Trojan ranks.
Aias kills Hippothous as he drags the corpse, and Phorcys; Apollo, disguised, rouses Aeneas to rally the wavering Trojans.
Aias holds the line as both sides tug Patroclus's corpse like a stretched oxhide, fighting on in Zeus's dark mist.
Achilles does not yet know Patroclus is dead; his immortal horses weep apart until Zeus pities and revives them.
Automedon fights on alone till Alcimedon takes the reins; Hector, spotting the horses, summons Aeneas to help seize them.
Automedon prays and kills Aretus with a spear-cast; the Aiantes arrive as Athena descends to rouse the Achaeans.
Athena, as Phoenix, emboldens Menelaus, who kills Podes son of Eetion; Apollo, disguised, spurs the grieving Hector onward.
Zeus's aegis and thunder rout the Achaeans, wounding several; Aias, sensing Zeus's hand, prays for clear skies to see.
Zeus clears the battle-mist at Aias's prayer; Aias sends Menelaus to find Antilochus and warn Achilles of the death.
Antilochus, grief-stricken, runs to tell Achilles; Aias has Menelaus and Meriones lift Patroclus's body while the Aiantes cover their retreat.
The Aiantes, like a headland stemming a flood, hold off the pursuing Trojans under Aeneas and Hector as Achaeans flee.

books.argument: Achilles mourns Patroclus, routs Trojans unarmed at the trench, and Thetis secures him new armor.

scenes.summary: Antilochus brings Achilles news that Patroclus is dead; Achilles collapses in grief, defiling his face with dust.
Thetis, hearing her son's cry from the sea, rises in lament with her chorus of Nereid sisters.
Thetis comforts Achilles, who vows to kill Hector in revenge though he knows it seals his own death.
Thetis warns that Achilles's own death follows swiftly after Hector's; Achilles accepts fate to win glory avenging his friend.
Thetis promises new armor from Hephaestus by dawn and departs for Olympus while her sisters return to the sea.
Hector nearly drags off Patroclus's corpse until Iris, sent secretly by Hera, urges unarmed Achilles to intervene.
Achilles, wreathed in fire and Athena's aegis, shouts from the trench, routing the Trojans in terror.
The Achaeans recover Patroclus's body and lay him on a bier as the sun sets, ending the day's battle.
The Trojans hold a fearful night assembly; Polydamas urges retreat within the walls before Achilles can attack at dawn.
Hector rejects Polydamas's counsel, scorning retreat, and vows to face Achilles openly at dawn outside the walls.
Achilles leads the Myrmidons in nightlong lament over Patroclus and has the body washed and anointed for burial.
Zeus and Hera spar over her success in rousing Achilles against the Trojans.
Thetis reaches Hephaestus's bronze palace on Olympus and is welcomed by Charis while he forges golden tripods.
Thetis begs Hephaestus, who owes her a debt from infancy, to forge new armor for doomed Achilles.
Hephaestus promises magnificent armor and sets his bellows to work, gathering bronze, tin, silver, and gold.
Hephaestus forges the shield's cosmic field, a wedding and a lawsuit, and a besieged city with an ambush.
The shield depicts plowland, a king's harvest, a golden vineyard, dancers, and a herd of cattle attacked by lions.
Hephaestus completes the shield with a dancing-floor and Ocean's stream, then forges corselet, helm, and greaves for Thetis.

books.argument: Achilles ends his wrath, receives divine armor, and returns to battle after mourning Patroclus.

scenes.summary: Dawn breaks; Thetis brings Achilles new armor from Hephaestus and vows to keep Patroclus's corpse from decay.
Achilles summons the Achaeans; wounded Diomedes, Odysseus, and Agamemnon limp to the assembly.
Achilles publicly renounces his wrath against Agamemnon and urges the army to battle at once.
Agamemnon blames Ate for the quarrel, recounts Zeus's deception at Heracles's birth, and offers restitution.
Odysseus counsels the army to eat before battle and urges Agamemnon to present the gifts and swear his oath.
Agamemnon orders the gifts and Briseis brought forward; Achilles refuses food, vowing to fast until Hector falls.
Odysseus insists the weary army must eat before fighting; Achilles yields and lets the gift-bearers go.
Agamemnon's gifts and Briseis are delivered; he sacrifices a boar to Zeus and swears he never touched her.
The Myrmidons store the gifts; Briseis finds Patroclus's body and laments him and her own slain kin.
Achilles refuses to eat, grieving for Patroclus and fearing for his aged father and young son at home.
Zeus pities the fasting Achilles and sends Athena to feed him nectar and ambrosia unseen.
The Achaeans arm for war; Achilles dons Hephaestus's armor and takes up his father's ash spear.
Automedon yokes the immortal horses; Achilles charges Xanthus and Balius to bring him home alive.
Given human speech by Hera, Xanthus foretells Achilles's death; Achilles accepts his fate and drives to battle.

books.argument: The gods join the war as Achilles duels Aeneas and rampages through the Trojan ranks.

scenes.summary: Zeus convenes the gods and permits them to intervene in the battle on either side.
The gods take sides and descend to battle; Poseidon's earthquake shakes Olympus, earth, and the underworld.
Apollo, disguised as Lycaon, spurs Aeneas to face Achilles; Hera rallies Poseidon and Athena to intervene.
Achilles and Aeneas meet between the armies; Achilles taunts him over rumored Trojan kingship.
Aeneas answers with his full genealogy from Dardanus through Priam and Anchises before charging.
Achilles and Aeneas duel with spears; Achilles draws his sword as Aeneas seizes a boulder.
Poseidon pities Aeneas, shrouds Achilles in mist, and lifts Aeneas from the field to safety.
Achilles, mist cleared, marvels at Aeneas's escape and rallies the Achaeans against the Trojans.
Hector vows to face Achilles, but Apollo warns him to wait within the throng.
Achilles kills Iphition, Demoleon, Hippodamas, and Priam's son Polydorus.
Hector charges to avenge Polydorus; Athena turns aside his spear, and Apollo hides him in mist.
Achilles slaughters more Trojans in a rampage, his hands and chariot drenched in gore.

books.argument: Achilles slaughters Trojans at the Scamander, battles the river, and nears Troy's walls.

scenes.summary: Achilles splits the fleeing Trojans, driving many into the river Xanthus, and cuts them down.
Exhausted from slaughter, Achilles seizes twelve Trojan youths alive as a blood-price for Patroclus.
Fleeing the river unarmed, Priam's son Lycaon meets Achilles, who once sold and ransomed him.
Lycaon clasps Achilles's knees and begs for his life as a former suppliant guest-friend.
Achilles refuses ransom, kills Lycaon, and flings his body into the river with a taunt.
Achilles kills Asteropaeus, son of the river-god Axius, after an exchange of spear-casts.
Achilles slaughters fleeing Paeonians until the river Scamander, choked with corpses, protests.
Achilles defies the river's warning and keeps killing; Scamander rises against him in flood.
Nearly drowned, Achilles prays to Zeus; Poseidon and Athena reassure him he will not die here.
Scamander calls on the river Simois for aid and surges again to overwhelm Achilles.
Hera sends Hephaestus, who scorches the plain and the riverbanks with fire to master the flood.
The river begs for mercy, and Hera bids Hephaestus quench his flame.
The gods clash: Ares strikes Athena, who fells him with a stone; Aphrodite is struck leading him away.
Poseidon spars with Apollo, who withdraws; Artemis, mocked by Hera, is beaten with her own bow.
Apollo enters Troy to guard its wall while the other gods return to Olympus.
Achilles keeps slaughtering; Priam orders the gates opened to receive the routed Trojans.
Apollo rouses Agenor to face Achilles, then lures Achilles from the gates as Trojans flee inside.

books.argument: Achilles chases Hector around Troy's walls, kills him, and drags his body toward the ships.

scenes.summary: Apollo unveils himself to Achilles, rebuking his pursuit of a god; Achilles turns back toward Troy.
Priam sees Achilles coming and begs Hector to retreat inside the walls, naming his lost sons.
Hecuba bares her breast, pleading with Hector to face Achilles safely from behind the wall.
Alone at the gates, Hector debates retreat, negotiation, and combat, and resolves to fight.
Terror seizes Hector as Achilles closes in; he flees, and the chase around Troy begins.
The gods watch the chase; Zeus weighs sparing Hector, then lets fate decide; the scales sink for him.
Athena tells Achilles to rest while she lures Hector into a stand disguised as Deiphobus.
Deceived, Hector agrees to face Achilles together with the false Deiphobus.
Hector and Achilles exchange spear-casts; Hector's missile fails, and he finds Deiphobus gone.
Hector realizes Athena's trick and charges with his sword; Achilles spears him through the throat.
Dying, Hector begs for his body's return and foretells Achilles's death; Achilles refuses and gloats.
Achaeans stab Hector's corpse; Achilles strips his armor and mutilates the body, binding it to his chariot.
Achilles drags Hector's body toward the ships as Priam and Hecuba watch and wail from the walls.
Unaware at her loom, Andromache hears the cries, sees Hector dragged, and laments his and Astyanax's fate.

books.argument: The Achaeans cremate Patroclus overnight and hold funeral games the next day in his honor.

scenes.summary: The army returns to camp; Achilles keeps the Myrmidons armed, circling Patroclus's body three times in mourning.
Achilles vows to sacrifice twelve Trojan youths and feed Hector to dogs; a funeral feast follows.
Achilles refuses to bathe until Patroclus is buried and asks Agamemnon to gather wood for the pyre.
That night Patroclus's ghost visits the sleeping Achilles, begging for swift burial and shared bones.
At dawn Agamemnon sends men and mules under Meriones to fetch wood from Mount Ida.
The armed Myrmidons escort Patroclus's body in procession, their shorn hair covering the corpse.
Achilles cuts a lock of hair vowed to the river Spercheius and gives it to Patroclus instead.
Achilles dismisses the wider host and, with the chief mourners, builds a great pyre for the body.
Achilles sacrifices sheep, oxen, horses, dogs, and twelve Trojan captives on the pyre for Patroclus.
The pyre will not catch; Achilles prays to the winds, which come and burn it through the night.
At dawn the fire dies; the Achaeans quench it, gather Patroclus's bones into a golden urn, and raise a barrow.
Achilles sets prizes for a chariot race; Nestor advises his son Antilochus on rounding the turning-post.
The chariot race runs; Apollo and Athena intervene, and Diomedes finishes first, ahead of Antilochus and Menelaus.
Antilochus's reckless driving nearly costs Menelaus second place; Achilles adds a prize and settles their quarrel.
Nestor receives an honorary prize and recalls his own youthful victories at Amarynceus's funeral games.
Epeius knocks out Euryalus with a single blow to win the boxing match.
Telamonian Aias and Odysseus wrestle to a draw; Achilles stops the match and awards them equal prizes.
In the footrace, Athena trips Oïlean Aias to let Odysseus win; Antilochus praises Achilles's own speed.
Telamonian Aias and Diomedes duel in armor for a sword; the Achaeans halt the contest for Aias's safety.
Achilles holds contests in weight-throwing, archery, and javelin, honoring Polypoetes, Meriones, Teucer, and Agamemnon.

books.argument: The gods relent; Priam ransoms Hector's body from Achilles by night, and Troy buries him.

scenes.summary: Each night Achilles drags Hector's body around Patroclus's tomb, though Apollo shields it from harm.
On the twelfth day, Apollo protests the gods' cruelty in letting Achilles abuse Hector's corpse.
Hera argues Hector deserves less honor than goddess-born Achilles; Zeus insists both were dear to him.
Zeus sends Iris to summon Thetis, telling her Achilles must return Hector's body for ransom.
Thetis delivers Zeus's command to the grieving Achilles, who agrees to accept ransom for Hector.
Zeus sends Iris to Priam, instructing him to ransom Hector alone with Hermes as his guide.
Priam tells Hecabe of the divine message; she begs him not to go, but he insists.
Priam gathers rich robes, gold, and vessels as ransom, driving his grieving household away in anger.
Priam prays for a sign, receives a favorable eagle omen, and sets out with the herald Idaeus.
At dusk near Ilus's tomb, Priam and Idaeus halt to water the animals as Hermes draws near.
Disguised as a young squire, Hermes reassures the frightened Priam and offers to guide him to Achilles.
Hermes lulls the Achaean sentries to sleep and leads Priam's wagon unseen into the camp.
Unseen, Priam enters Achilles's hut, clasps his knees, and begs him by his own father's grief.
Moved to tears for his father and Patroclus, Achilles raises Priam and speaks of mortal sorrow.
Achilles agrees to free Hector's body, which is washed, anointed, and laid on a bier unseen.
Achilles and Priam share a meal, and Achilles pledges to hold back the army for eleven days.
The household sleeps, but Hermes wakes Priam before dawn to slip unseen from the camp.
At dawn Priam nears Troy with Hector's body; Cassandra spies them and raises the city's lament.
Hector's body is borne into Troy; Andromache, Hecuba, and Helen each lead the lament over him.
The Trojans gather wood for nine days, cremate Hector on the tenth, and bury him on the eleventh.
